projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joseph Walter Michalec was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran, Joseph Walter Michalec. Mr. Michalec served in the U.S. Navy with the Amphibious Force. Joseph served in the Pacific Campaign. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Michalec's home in Metro, Ohio on January 9th, 2003. Joe was 81 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Fall River, Massachusetts. No. Pardon me. I got that wrong. I was living in Norwich, Connecticut.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you in school?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Had you joined the Navy at that point?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. You were in the Navy, right; I got that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. All right. So do you have memories of December 7th, the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Very vivid memories.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me as much as you can about that.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, we were at a lunch counter having some coffee and donuts when we heard a radio message that the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor. It was about 1:00 in the afternoon then; but it was after coming from church; and we went to our mass, and...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard the news?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, we didn't even know much about Pearl Harbor. We knew about Hawaii. We used to listen to Bing Crosby make Sunday evening broadcast from Hawaii, and we knew about Hawaii, but we didn't know Pearl Harbor was such an important base; but we knew that the Japanese were negotiating. Then we remembered a Columbus Day fire at the Firestone factory where a lot of rubber got burned. And they claimed that might have been a sabotage by the Japanese, because at that time there was very little synthetic rubber in the United States, and that was a big strategic product for us; because most of the rubber was -- raw rubber was brought from rubber plantations in the -- that's Dutch east in -- Dutch --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: East Indies?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: In the East Indies, yeah. That's where all the rubber plantations were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did they ever find out anything for certain of whether that was sabotaged?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: No, they didn't, not that I know of; but we watched the big rubber blocks tumbling out of the factory burning.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So I -- it didn't -- it wasn't totally unexpected, then, when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, no. No. A lot of people were talking about Japanese might attack already.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, you -- did you say you were with your buddies when you heard the news?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we were in a restaurant.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you tempted to go out and sign up?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, not right -- right then and there. It took a while for us. Then they started -- they had a draft already. Guys were already being inscripted, but I didn't think about getting in right away. It took a couple of months before I made up my mind. I said, well, more and more of my buddies were being drafted. I said, well, I better get in. I always liked the Navy, but before the war, you had to be a high school graduate to get in the Navy. And I didn't graduate from high school. But I figured, well, this is my chance to get in the Navy if I join. I'd rather be in the Navy than the Army, so I signed up in the Navy July of '42.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, I was in Norwich, Connecticut, working for Singer selling sewing machines then, and I enlisted in a recruiting station in Norwich. Went to Newhaven for a physical and was sworn in there ten days later, because they gave us ten days to get our things in order, report back to get sworn in. Then we went to Newport for our boot training. The next six weeks through boot training there at Newport Training Station, the regular -- but they speeded it up, naturally, during wartime. Usually the naval training program was about three months. And for us, it was about eight weeks. And then we shipped -- I was shipped down to -- they chose me for diesel school down in Richmond, Virginia. I was disappointed because some of my friends went immediately to sea duty aboard ship. Then I heard 17 of my company were sunk on a ship a month later and drowned by a German submarine, and I thought, well, maybe I was lucky to be picked for diesel school. Then from there, from Richmond, I went -- was sent to Cleveland to General Motors diesel school. Because I did well at Richmond diesel, they sent me up to Cleveland General Motors diesel. Went to school there for I think it was two months. Then they shipped us down to Solomons, Maryland, where our school training was complete, and we were formed into crews for amphibious craft, landing craft. I was assigned to a tank landing craft. And then we started training with troops, the Marines, and landing maneuvers on Chesapeake Bay. Then we went to training with LSTs, Virginia Beach, and places like that, on LSTs and on Amphtrac landing crafts. Then we were shipped from there, after a couple of months, down to New Orleans and did some more training down there. Then we had wound up aboard an LST to landing craft, a tank landing craft was put aboard an LST, and went down through Panama, and we stopped at Cocosolo. That was a Marine base in Panama. We had to stop for traffic going through the canal. Stayed there two or three days and moved a couple of liberties at Cologne and San Cristobal.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything exciting down there, any memories --

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, just -- oh, well, we went to bars there. We were excited about getting steaks down there real cheap and whiskey real cheap. And the thing about it down there, they'd place a whiskey bottle in front of you on the bar. They didn't pour you the shot, but -- and the bartender would walk away, but he'd come back and he'd ask, "How many drinks did you have?" and you'd tell him, but he -- he would know. He was -- he could just look at the bottle and tell. And we didn't lie about it, but you'd pay him for the drinks you had. You'd say two or three, whatever. And he'd pour you one and walk away again, but he -- you didn't want to lie because you -- he -- he could tell. He was -- that was odd. And then we'd buy green bananas, a whole stock of them for about a quarter and hang them up in -- aboard ship. They'd ripen aboard ship. Have them later on. That was a lot of fun, coming to thinking about it was fun. And we bought souvenirs down there. And coming up on the West Coast, we'd stop San Diego, and we had maneuvers there to practice around San Clemente, Camp Pendleton, with the Marines. We did landing maneuvers and then we did towing targets, planes strafing runs and bombing runs and stuff like that. Then we went down -- went down to Tijuana and had that thing drawn up by a -- one of them starving artists for a dollar, had that charcoal sketch. And, well, we run around San Diego, went to the zoos and stuff down there. Went to Ocean City amusement -- no. There's no amusement park there. We went to the bars there, in Ocean City. Then we almost got shot returning back to Camp Pendleton. Large part of the base was restricted area. We were drinking and we got drunk. We started walking through -- back to the docks to get on our craft, and some guy hollered, "Halt." We didn't pay no attention _____+ and we heard the click of the rifle. And then we stopped. He said, "We're just going back to the docks." He said, "Stay right there." We said, "We're going back to the docks." He said, "Didn't you see the sign, restricted area?" Oh, he said, "You ain't supposed to be here." I don't know what was there. Something we weren't supposed to see. He told us to get the hell out of this area. He said, "You'll get shot over here." So anyway, then we went -- from there we went -- we'd gone up to San Francisco. We had what they call a typhoon, like a hurricane, and washed up on a beach at San Simeon, just below the Hearst Castle. We spent Christmas Eve on a beach there, washed up on a beach on that tank landing craft. We had to wait three days for a Navy tugboat to come take us off. And we -- up to San Francisco, they put us in dry dock in Oakland. I spent New Year's Eve in San Francisco on Market Street which is like Times Square in New York. I went to Chinatown for a Chinese dinner, New Year's Eve. The next day, I was going back to Oakland. I see a street car filling up with people and nobody getting off. And your uniform was your admission for any -- you didn't pay for anything. I said, "Where the hell are these people going?" I think I'll go see where they're going. I still had a day's liberty. So I got on the street car with them, and I got off in front of this great big stadium. I asked the guy, "What's going on here?" He looked at me like I was a moron. He said, "It's the East-West Game. Don't you know that?" I says, "Well" -- "what" -- he's -- I said, "Football?" He said, "Yeah. That's Kezar Stadium, the East-West New Year's game." "Oh," I said. So I went and seen the game. They tied the score that year, '44. New Year's Day 1944, 6-6. I still got the program. I was there someplace. Then -- but we did some ferrying duty back and forth across the Bay for the Navy, loading ships with ammunition and stuff. Then we had final repairs done, and then they put us aboard an LST and we headed for Hawaii. And we did some three months training over there. And May 21st, I think it was May 21st, we had -- we thought was sabotage. We lost two LSTs in big explosions. Somebody said a guy dropped a box of detonators with caps or something. Anyway, the LST, about a dozen of them were tied up next to each other and all getting loaded, combat loaded, for invasions, and one of them blew up and they went off like firecrackers. A lot of guys got killed and we spent two days pulling bodies out of the harbor. They had to tow the burning LSTs out to the sea and sink them. It was terrible, went on for about three or four days. And then we took off for -- we didn't know where the hell we were going, of course, but the next stop was _____+ was June 6th, and we heard over the radio about the Normandy Invasion, that they landed in Europe. And we made a stop at Argolian, and then we hit Saipan the 15th, the morning of the 15th. It was the 14th here. It was the 15th there. And the day before, the chaplain passed out rosary. I remember this guy, Bill Ipiska (ph), he's a Marine from Pittsburgh. These rosaries were made out of chord. Instead of beads, they had knots made. You know, Red Cross had -- I guess some nuns someplace made these rosaries. They were made out of chord. Instead of beads, they had knots, for the -- for, you know, the spots. And this Bill Ipiska says, "Hey, will you show me how to make _____+ rosaries?" I said, "Yeah." Because he was going to hit the beach, first one, the first wave. And I showed -- I never heard -- saw him no more but I remember his name. I had his picture but I lost it. He gave me his picture. He told me if I get through, to get in touch with his family, but I never had an address or nothing, so I never did. And then we secured Saipan. And then about middle of July, about the same time they secured Guam, we hit Tinian. Secured that. And then I was there until October 13th, just -- we went through several air raids. Then -- they weren't as bad as the typhoon we had there. We had a bad typhoon. Lost a couple of destroyers. They were washed up on a beach and got smashed up on the rocks. And several air raids, strange things we went through. During that typhoon, we went out about a mile and a half, and we dropped our hook. And we set the cable. We tightened it, but we let some slack in the cable so it would give, so it wouldn't snap. That's what happened to the destroyers -- they set the -- is broke the chains and that's -- they hit -- got washed up on the beach; but we had an anchor watch, the watch would let -- watch the cable gradually slip out. When it got close to the end, we'd reel it in again, and just give it enough slack so it would pay out. And I was there till I got hurt during a bombing raid. I got my head cut open, and I went to -- we only had -- I had -- the comfort was there, the hospital shift, but they were loaded with Marines. One of the guys got hurt on the ship one day during a raid. My shipmate -- bullet scraped his ear, and I took him aboard. They fixed that in the comfort. But it was so loaded with Marines, I went -- when I got hurt, I went to the field hospital on the -- Saipan. And I remember the doctor's name was Dr. Striker, a German guy. He stitched me up and said, "You got to stay overnight for observation." I says, "Well, I got to go back. I'm the only one that can run my barge. I can run engines." He says, "Well, can you come back in the morning?" I said, "Yeah." But when I got back, the skipper says, "Pack your gear. You're going back to the States." So I didn't tell him the doctor told me come back in the morning.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how exactly did you get hurt?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: During a bombing raid, we had a near miss and I fell back against a gun or something, a 20-millimeter gun, the edge of it like that. I cracked the back of my head. I had four stitches in it. I took the four stitches back myself -- out myself. I went back on the Moore McGrand (ph). That was the -- Moore-McCormack lines. They -- that was the Moore-McCormack shipbuilding company in San Fran -- because they called them Moore McGrandy (ph). They named them after birds. We had 800 troops on the -- they brought out the cargo. They send them into true -- compartments, five bunks hiding in cargo holes. Had 800 troops on there. I went back to the States, you know, rotating. And so I got back to the States November -- I left there October 13. We went on a score that took us 29 days to get back to San Francisco, because we were going zigzag, dodging submarines. Got back to the States November 14th. I told you we couldn't go -- immediately leave, 30 days, but I told them I didn't have no money but I did. I didn't draw no pay. I had $3,000. For all the time I was in the Pacific, I didn't draw any pay; but I told them I had to wait until the next pay period. In the meantime, I wanted to be home for Christmas. I left November 14th. Have to come back December -- I wanted to be home for Christmas. So meantime, I got sick. I had dingy fever for three day -- but dingy fever is like malaria, but it don't stay like malaria. You get it three days. You get over it. So I got sick. In the hospital, they tell me I fell asleep and they woke me up. There's a _____, a nurse and a senior medical officer, a chaplain, they say, "Got bad news for you." "What's the bad news?" What the hell are they going to tell me, am I going to die or what? Said, "First, I want to check you out," the medical officer said. "Well, take your gown off." I said, "There's a lady here." "That's all right. She's a nurse." I was embarrassed. They checked me out. Said, "All right, Chaplain, you tell him." Chaplain says, "Your father passed away." And he said, "Where are you from, son?" I said, "Fall River, Massachusetts." He says, "Oh, Fall River?" He says, "I'm from Fall River. I'm Father Keller." I says _____+ St. Louis. I says, "I'm from Holy Cross." "Oh." He was from my same hometown, the chaplain. "Well, what do you want to do?" I said, "Well, I want to go home." They got -- they said I could have a Navy plane free of charge but I have to wait 24 hours. I said, "Well, can I get a civilian plane?" They got me a priority. I paid for the plane. It was $168. Well, we only got as far as Pittsburgh because there was a snowstorm. I took a train but I made it just in time. They had the casket in the church already. The funeral mass was on. My mother couldn't keep it off any longer. And they opened the casket at the church and at the cemetery so I could see my father before they put him away. So I made it home. And after that, I went back and I went to -- I went to commission -- I went down -- where the heck -- oh, yeah. I went back to Little Creek. I got married to a lady -- Navy chaplain. And my wife come -- and I went to commission LSMR. That's where -- that's that picture there. It was going to be a rocket ship. And in the war, I did and I got discharged.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But before that, you were on an LCT?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, what was your --

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: That's a landing craft tank.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When was your particular job on there?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: I was their diesel machinist. I was operating an engine room, running the engines, operating the ramp, letting it down, and running the whole engine room.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many landings were you involved in then?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, about four.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any specific memories about those landings?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: A very vivid -- actual invasions, there was only two, like in Saipan and Tinian, but we were ferrying constantly. You go out -- because they didn't have no docks or nothing, just the big transport ships. You have to go out. We brought in tanks, guns, bulldozers, those mats that they made for the airplanes on the airports. Like when they -- when we got to Tinian, we had to bring all them mats for the runways for the planes and everything, anything they needed: bulldozers, Jeeps. There's another memory. We had this beach commander they called "Sweeny" Anderson. We took one load and then we had two big 155-millimeter guns. They called them long-time rifles that they used for barrage purposes. They lost a Jeep. The Jeep left -- come off the ramp. We were out about, oh, maybe 50 feet in the water from shore, and the Jeep hit a mine and blew up. So the captain and Marine said, "Hey, hold it." He's holding the guys up. They wanted to get some guys out there to see if there's any more mines. And Sweeny Anderson come running by, says, "Hey, what the hell's the holdup?" I said, look, the captain said we just lost a Jeep. He says, "You lost a Jeep?" He says, "You want to stop the whole God damned war? Get out of there." {Laughing} He says, "You don't stop the war for one Jeep."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: You know, there's a lot going on. You -- your particular problem don't mean nothing, you know, overall. For you, it does. It just like somebody telling you when you go into the hospital, oh, that's a minor operation. Like hell. To you, it's minor. To me, it's major. You know what I mean?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: If it's you -- you're the one that's involved, it's a major thing. So that's the way it used to be there, too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Which landing was that, when that happened?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: In Tinian.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was at Tinian?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: And things we'd be scared -- like, the strays would be shooting over the head, you know, and they'd hit something, and the damn thing -- whole damn thing would blow up, come over your head. You couldn't see nothing, but it would be shooting at you. But it'd hit maybe a big -- whatever, munitions or something was piled up somewhere on the -- in the floor all over you. And you wonder what the hell's coming at you now. Yeah, things was pretty rough. And then one day was really scary. After we hit Saipan, that was, I think, the day that Mariana's Turkey Shoot -- you probably heard of that one -- well, we were hit -- we hit the beach about the second or third day, I forget, because everything -- it was just too much excitement going on, shelling, you were -- you see the shells flying over you day and night. And one night, we -- one evening, like you look out, like you look over the lake, sometimes when the fishing -- were boats out there or the ice -- ice fishers sometime went out, you blink, it looks like a city out there. Well, that was the way it was -- and that with lights; but before dark, you see the ships, so many ships out there like you could step on -- next morning, when it got light, not a damn thing out there. Said, "What the hell happened?" We only had a 500-mile range. You know, we couldn't go nowhere. We thought, oh, shit. Now we're stuck here. The Japs must have chased them all away. And that was when they sent all the -- chased the ship -- the Japs got through. What we found out later was this Jap task force was coming down and that's when we got them. That's -- that's when they shot all them planes down and stopped them; but they sent all them -- that invasion for us out back in case they did get through. Because if they got through, they would have been able to get all them transports and everything.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they --

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: They sent them out of harm's way, but they didn't get through. So eventually, two or three days later, they started slowly coming back. Boy, what a relief that was for us, because we didn't have any fresh water for any length of time or anything else, you know. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were stranded on the beach basically, right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, sure. Yeah, well, just like you're stuck out there thousands of miles from your nearest American help that you can get, you know, if things didn't work out, that's the way they did it. But then we heard about all the planes they shot down and the ships started coming back. Things started shaping up. Planes started coming in. The B-29s started coming in. Then we heard about the raids they pulled. Then we heard about Iwo Jima. B-51s were coming in and Mustangs. When that -- all that started happening, we knew that we were going to be okay then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other memories of that, of Saipan?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, I know about Garanpanoa (ph) and Charan Kanoa and Garapan, rather, and Charan Kanoa, the sugar mill, the natives there, the Chamorros. We walked around there. Oh, we went hiking there. I had a .45 Carbine and a sidearm. We went in groups though. And one time we found a couple of bottles of saki, and we drank that. And then we heard a broadcast over the radio, be careful about drinking any liquor or anything you might find because they booby trapped it. They put poison in it. So we were worried as hell, you know, what the hell is going to happen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you were okay?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That broadcast was from -- from on our side, American --

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Yeah. Well, from the Navy, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It wasn't from Tokyo Rose?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, no. We heard broadcasts from her, too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did -- what did she have to say?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, "We're waiting for you. We know you're coming. We're waiting for you." But -- "It'd be wise to turn back because we're all ready for you," and stuff like that. Then we heard a lot from her. Played nice music and everything, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that why you kept listening to her, because of the music?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't care what she had to say if it was propaganda --

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Guys used to make fun of her. "I'd like to go to bed with you, Babe," and stuff, because she sounded sexy, you know. You know, guys, they made fun of her. They didn't pay no attention. Just like that Axis Sally in Europe. Took it with a grain of salt. They didn't -- she didn't have any effect on the guys as far as propaganda goes. They can't do -- GIs, you know, GIs, they'll -- they'll get what they can out of somebody but they ain't -- you ain't going to make a Nazi out of a GI or a Jap out of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your rank?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Chief petty officer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other particular memories of that time over there?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about buddies?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, all dead. Joe Murdoch was one of my best buddies. He was my shipmate. I wanted to go see him, he lived in North Bend, Oregon, when I visited my boys in Seattle, but he died at 57. And the guys I remembered, they're all scattered out, all from down south to _____. I remember them all but I never got to see them or nothing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long were you on Saipan, then?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, from June 15th till October 13th, 14th.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And Tinian, how long were you there?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, Tinian and Saipan both -- both are close together.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: They're all part of the Marianas. So Marianas, Guam, Saipan, Tinian, they're all grouped together just like Hawaii. I was there from June to October.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: October of '40 --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Do you have memories of mail call, getting letters from home?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Used to get mail all the time from my wife. Of course, we were only dating them. She used to get my letters. We had PBYs come out there all the time with mail, the PBY Catalina. Boy, they'd come in bunches. It wasn't regularly. My wife used to tell me that the postman used to laugh at her. She was working for these -- because she's from Europe. She was working for some people in Shaker Square. Postman used to kid her. He said, "How many boyfriends you get?" because she'd get seven or eight letters at a time. I'd write a letter every day. There was nothing else to do out there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would you write about?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Mostly just tell her that I -- she'd get letters, some parts of the letters cut out. They didn't just black them up, they cut them all out. It wasn't much you could write about. Just say you're feeling okay and things are going okay or be back soon, stuff like that. Even pictures. Sometime I'd take -- get some pictures made in Hawaii, when I was in Hawaii, sometime it'd go through, sometime they wouldn't. Sometime they would confiscate them. Sometime they didn't. Same ones, I'd have -- I'd bring -- I'd take them to a developer. I'd get them back. Next time they'd come back censored, confiscated. I don't know what the hell. You know, I'd take them when we were training out there, or I'd take pictures of the beach, of the troops landing or something. I'd get some and some I wouldn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Would they return those pictures when they confiscated them?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They just took them away?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Just took the negative and everything. Just a note: "Pictures confiscated by sensor."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would she write to you?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, just she missed me, you know how the kids write.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Miss each other. "I miss you. Wish you could come home." They tell you about, "Oh, I found some silk stockings today." Oh, we had some of this today. Her and her girlfriend, they'd see a line. They'd be, "I wonder what's in there, in the line?" They get in line. They didn't know what the hell they're in line for. It was during the war. Things were rationed, you know. When I was in Mexico, I bought her some silver stuff, broaches, a broach and some -- a bracelet and stuff. Oh, she was so thrilled with that. I sent it to her. And stuff was cheap down in Mexico. And silver, they were very good silver artists and it was cheap. I bought her some things like that, trinkets.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You mentioned that one air raid where you got hurt. Do you have any other memories of air raids?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We were getting them all the time. But now, they kept diminishing. At first, they were pretty rough, but they kept diminishing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No other close calls for you?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, I've heard about the fanatical Japanese resistance of Saipan. Did you witness any of that? A. Oh, yeah. _____+ They were -- they would come by and some of the guys, they'd even get on some of the barges and stuff. I heard of guys being attacked at night and stuff right on the barges, but it never happened to us on our barge. Yeah, they -- I seen bodies around, and I seen machine gun -- seen guys machine-gunning boats trying to go from Saipan to Tinian. At first, they used to try to rescue them. A lot of them, Saipan and Tinian are close together, and some of them Japanese would -- when they were securing -- Saipan was almost secured, they tried to escape over to Tinian. Well, they'd machine-gun them. Then when they'd fall in the water, they tried to rescue them. But them guys would come out with knives and stab the rescuers. So the commander says, "Hey, the hell with them. Just shoot them. We're not going to risk any more guys getting stabbed." He says, "Get rid of them." They wouldn't take the chance. You'd see bodies floating around there. And I'd see them on the beaches, too. They'd bulldoze them in the -- just bulldoze them down. But it smelled and stank all the time over there. Bodies. Yeah, I can still smell that all the time. Never get rid of that smell.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you must have had a bittersweet reunion with your family then because the first time you saw them was at the funeral?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah, my dad passed away. Ain't the worst thing that could happen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Your mom was glad to see you, though, I bet? A. Oh, yeah. Mostly it was sad because my dad thought I would be the one but he survived a couple of wars himself in Poland, but he went before I did. He got double pneumonia, got a bad cold and didn't take care of it, turned into pneumonia. And, you know, in '44, there wasn't the medicine and stuff they have now. And, you know, he wouldn't see a doctor and he should have. I talked to his doctor. He said he had bilateral pneumonia and his lungs were full of fluid. If he had got help sooner, he might have helped him but he was too late. They put him in an oxygen tank but they couldn't help him no more. But that's the way them old-timers were, you know. I don't think he ever saw a doctor in his life.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you were overseas, did you get any shows of any sort, USO things? A. Oh, yeah, we saw several shows. I forget who they're -- mostly most of them shows are not that you see -- they went to the officers' clubs, and there were the nurses in there, and they had dances. But that was put on -- yeah, they had a few shows for the enlisted men. They were packed in like sardines. You would see them. Boot camp, we had some nice movies. We -- I saw Holiday Inn. That's where they first introduced the song White Christmas in September of '42. That's before it was shown in the theaters. Saw that in boot camp in September of '42. And that wasn't out in the movies until later.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: That's when White Christmas was first --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: -- out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've seen the movie.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Holiday Inn.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It's a great movie. When you think about that experience overseas, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: I enjoyed Hawaii more than anything else because I spent a lot of time there, three months. Maui, I spent time on. Did some swimming party -- we had some swimming parties there. I hiked around there. And I road horseback around Waikiki Beach and Diamond Head, because we had daytime liberty only. We had nighttime curfew. We had to be back at 6:00 because they had blackouts there all the time. No lights after nightfall. And they had island whiskey there, so -- and then gin joints were rip-offs for sale because we didn't have much money. I was second class then. I had only $78 a month. That didn't last long. I used to go to this stable. I used to ride horses when I was younger. At home, I used to ran horses. So for five bucks a day, I used to be able to get a horse and I had -- I liked this horse. I called him Windy. Well, his name was -- they called him Windy. I used to bring him carrots and stuff from the base. I had him take a ride on the beaches around Coco Head and Diamond Head, and ride all over the place. They'd get sick and tired sitting around the beach. I sat around the -- I drank beer at the Royal Hawaiian. That was the only hotel on the beach then, the Royal Hawaiian.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there any tension against the Japanese on Hawaii at that point?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, yeah, a lot because, you know, the -- there was a lot of Japanese living on Hawaii even before the war, and they felt that -- in fact, they knew that a lot of them Japanese were giving information to the Japanese about Pearl Harbor because they lived all around Pearl Harbor _____.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were stateside when they dropped the bomb right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you hear or think when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Well, I was happy. I said, well, no more guys are going to get killed. See, that's where I am. These were -- these were -- down here there were going to be rocket launchers. We just had that 5-inch. Here's my black gang. This is the engine room gang. They call that an LSMR landing ship, medium rocket. This is a commissioning officer. This is the exec -- this is the skipper. That's Chief_____. There were going to be three more chiefs. That's me. That's the communications officer. Oh, the navigation, fire control, the engineering and -- it's engineering officer here. That's the navigational officer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So was this sometime during the summer of '45, then?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Oh, this was -- yeah, August.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: August.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: August '45.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right at the same time --

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- they dropped the bomb.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Yeah. No, I just -- we just went on a shakedown cruise in the Gulf of Mexico. And then I had enough points in service, they -- see, they gave -- when a war ended, they determined discharge time by points and war -- I mean, wartime experience in action, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: Or you had 45 points, you got -- had -- eligible for discharge. I could have got a bonus for physically sign -- sign up again, but I -- well, I was married and my wife was anxious to have me home, so I got out. I would have had liked to stay in, to tell you the truth. I had a good rating, and I liked the Navy, but my wife was lonesome. She had a lot on her mind. Her family was in Europe, in Czechoslovakia. She was worried about them, and she went through a lot. So, she came here when she was 17 years old. It was hard for her. I figured, hell, I better go home, stay with her.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what did you like most about Navy life?

sp.speaker: Joseph Walter Michalec
sp.p: I liked the service. I just liked it, moving around, traveling, seeing different places. Because, hell, I didn't have no money. I didn't -- best way to travel is in the Navy. And I got to see things, you know, that I never saw before. I enjoyed traveling. And I used to get around and see things. END OF CD
